titleText.noteEn: On Wikipedia, semi-protection limits who can edit a page. The title text extends the joke by applying that technical page status to the United States Constitution.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cita can also mean an appointment or a quotation. In writing and research, it can name the reference that identifies a source supporting a claim.

example.es: El informe incluye una cita de una fuente fiable.
example.en: The report includes a citation from a reliable source.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Requerida describes one feminine person or thing. The ending changes to match what is described: requerido is masculine singular, and requeridos or requeridas are plural.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What Spanish editorial notice says that a claim needs a source?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use cita requerida: “citation needed” or “citation required.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is a conventional notice in collaborative reference writing, especially on Spanish Wikipedia. It is often displayed in brackets as [cita requerida]. Short notices commonly omit an article such as una.

example.es: El editor añadió «cita requerida» después de la afirmación.
example.en: The editor added “citation needed” after the claim.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: a Wikipedia sourcing warning turned into a real-world protest slogan
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Wikipedia editors attach a citation-needed warning to a claim whose source is missing or inadequate. The placard carries that editing convention into a political rally, challenging the speaker's claims as if the speech were editable wiki text.

regions.geometryRationale: Apple Vision returned no lines or tokens for the tilted blue placard, so this measured box covers its complete two-word text.

words.geometryRationale: OCR missed the tilted blue lettering; this measured box isolates CITA without including the following word.
OCR missed the tilted blue lettering; these three measured boxes follow the slope of the full word REQUERIDA without covering the protester's head.

applications.explanationEn: Cita requerida is the conventional two-word editorial warning printed on the placard.
Cita is feminine singular, so the describing form matches it with the feminine ending in requerida.
Cita names the thing first, and requerida follows it with the description.
